Q: Is long double in C++ an implementation of IEEE's binary128? A:

Is long double in C++ an implementation of IEEE's binary128?

No. C++ doesn't even require the use of IEEE-754 for floating-point types. See

  • Does the C++ standard specify anything on the representation of floating point numbers?
  • Is it safe to assume floating point is represented using IEEE754 floats in C?

Only since C++11 you can check if the platform uses IEEE-754 with std::numeric_limits<T>::is_iec559, although the 80-bit extended long double is also IEEE-754 compliant and is_iec559 will return true for it

Why defaulting to an 80-bit representation on some cases?

Because x87 supports the 80-bit IEEE-754 extended precision format. Some later platforms like Motorola 6888x, Intel i960 and old Sparc also support that type, so it makes sense for compilers to use it for long double instead of resorting to the much slower software emulation

That's also the reason PowerPC uses double-double for long double by default, because you can utilize the hardware double unit which makes operations much faster. Old NVIDIA CUDA cores didn't have hardware support for double, so many people used float-float for the bigger precision. See Emulating FP64 with 2 FP32 on a GPU

In case of Itanium where floating-point registers are 82-bit wide then long double would highly likely have the same width, with some padding for proper alignment to 128-bit

Most other architectures don't have hardware for floating-point types larger than 64 bits, therefore they chose the IEEE-754 quadruple-precision format for ease of implementation and better forward compatibility, since if one day support for 128-bit floating-point came to real hardware, it'll most likely be IEEE-754 quadruple-precision. Currently Sparc is the only architecture with hardware support for quadruple precision

That said, most compilers have options to change the underlying format for long double though. For example in GCC has -mlong-double-64/80/128 and -m96/128bit-long-double for x86 and -mabi=ibmlongdouble/ieeelongdouble for PowerPC

Q: Can a makefile contain UTF8 chracters? A:

Good times, bad times, you know I've had my share ♫

$ cat Makefile
m=吧
粒=哇
bad:; :  $粒  $m
good:;: $(粒) $m
$ make bad
:  \xb2\x92 吧
$ make good
: 哇 吧

When I stopped skimping on parenthesis (for single UTF-8 character variables, at least here on Linux,) my output finally became clear! ♪

Q: GCC vs Clang when packing array<uint8_t,N> into uint64_t A:

The disassembly output of clang is missleading.

All what the pack and hash functions do in the shown disassembly is to return a logical AND on the argument address, which appears rather to look like a place holder rather than actual code. If you try to give the compiler something it cannot infer anything on, e.g.

int main() {
    I a,b,c,d,e,f;
    std::cin >> a >> b >> c >> d >> e >> f;
    key_type aa{ a,b,c,d,e,f };
    std::cout << cast_and_shift::hash(aa);
}

what you get for the disassembly is:

main:
        push    rax
        mov     rdi, qword ptr [rip + std::cin@GOTPCREL]
        lea     rsi, [rsp + 6]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)@PLT
        lea     rsi, [rsp + 5]
        mov     rdi, rax
        [...]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)@PLT
        movzx   eax, byte ptr [rsp + 6]
        movzx   esi, byte ptr [rsp + 5]
        movzx   ecx, byte ptr [rsp + 4]
        movzx   edx, byte ptr [rsp + 2]
        movzx   edi, byte ptr [rsp + 1]
        shl     rdi, 40
        shl     rdx, 32
        movzx   r8d, byte ptr [rsp + 3]
        shl     r8d, 24
        shl     ecx, 16
        shl     esi, 8
        or      rsi, rax
        or      rsi, rcx
        or      rsi, r8
        or      rsi, rdx
        or      rsi, rdi
        mov     rdi, qword ptr [rip + std::cout@GOTPCREL]
        call    std::ostream& std::ostream::_M_insert<unsigned long>(unsigned long)@PLT
        xor     eax, eax
        pop     rcx
        ret

for clang and

main:
        sub     rsp, 24
        mov     edi, OFFSET FLAT:std::cin
        lea     rsi, [rsp+9]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)
        [...]
        call    std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>& std::operator>><char, std::char_traits<char>>(std::basic_istream<char, std::char_traits<char>>&, char&)
        movzx   esi, BYTE PTR [rsp+10]
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+11]
        mov     edi, OFFSET FLAT:std::cout
        sal     rax, 16
        sal     rsi, 8
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+9]
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+12]
        sal     rax, 24
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+13]
        sal     rax, 32
        or      rsi, rax
        movzx   eax, BYTE PTR [rsp+14]
        sal     rax, 40
        or      rsi, rax
        call    std::ostream& std::ostream::_M_insert<unsigned long>(unsigned long)
        xor     eax, eax
        add     rsp, 24
        ret

for gcc (similar for the mem_cpy version). Apart from inlining the functions (including the actual hashing algorithm) alltogether, both compilers seem to deliver equivalently quick code: https://godbolt.org/z/b9MoMeTv1

Q: What do you recommend to learn in 2026? A:

Keep iterating yourself especially when you get rejected, be realistic about your expectations, start small, learn the fundamentals of the tech you are interested in (I know it's hard, but persistence pays off). From my experience, do not send the same resume to different job applications, take the time to iterate based to what the job offer is looking for.

There's no wrong or right answer to what to learn in 2026, start with what you are interested in, read articles about it, and most importantly deep dive with the fundamentals.
